text: launch_store.py renders a config, sets up an admin account, and pulls an inventory baseline -- but it still runs silently and treats every failure the same way. This final lesson adds the Slack alert, handles failures deliberately, and packages the project to actually show someone.

Reusing the webhook pattern from the health-checks lesson, main now reports its outcome instead of only logging it. One alert either way -- never zero, and never more than one -- so whoever's on call knows the result without reading a log file.

The logging lesson taught catching a specific exception before a generic fallback, and the capstone is where that habit earns its keep. A failed user-setup step and a failed API call call for different responses, so separate except blocks tell the reader exactly where to look first.

Packaging the project for a portfolio means showing the thinking, not just the code: the real manual problem it replaces, why each design choice looks the way it does, and an honest list of what you'd add next. That tells an employer more about your judgment than a line-by-line walkthrough.

Across six chapters you went from your first bash function to a script that templates a config, sets up a server, calls an authenticated API, and alerts a team -- real automation, not toy examples. The next course in the path, Docker & Containers, picks up right where this one leaves off.
